paragraphs: Popular beaches in eastern Sydney were closed to the public after a dead young humpback whale washed ashore in a rocky bay.

Local authorities shut down swimming and surfing spots as a safety precaution and warned that the whale carcass is likely to attract sharks to the coastline. Emergency teams and local rangers face significant challenges trying to remove the body because the animal is in an advanced state of decomposition, and the rough ocean conditions make the area inaccessible for boats or heavy machinery. Community leaders and experts noted that with growing whale populations along the coast, such events are becoming more common. Indigenous rangers plan to perform cultural ceremonies to honor the whale, while scientists advise the public to stay out of the water and let nature take its course if retrieval remains impossible.

paragraphs: Officials closed famous Australian beaches after a dead young whale washed up on rocky shores near Sydney. Lifeguards shut the beaches to keep swimmers safe because the whale carcass can attract dangerous sharks.

Local teams are trying to figure out how to handle the situation, but removing the heavy animal is extremely difficult. The ocean is rough, and the body is already breaking down. Experts say that more whales are migrating along the coast this season, which makes these events more common.
Indigenous groups are preparing special cultural ceremonies to respect the animal. For now, local leaders ask people to stay away from the water until the coast is clear and safe again.

paragraphs: A dead whale washes up on the rocks near Sydney, Australia. Local leaders close nearby beaches to keep people safe. They are worried that the big dead animal will bring hungry sharks near the shore.

Workers cannot easily move the whale. The water is dangerous, and the rocks are sharp. Also, the body is already breaking down into parts. Experts say that many whales are swimming near the land this month.
Local people and rangers want to do a special ceremony for the animal. Leaders tell visitors not to swim in the sea right now.
